Super Blanky founder and CEO Karen Bonnici joins Bradley alongside her nephew and newest intern, Jack Lustig, to share the story behind the wearable blanket. After watching the children play with her original cape-style design, Karen developed its signature pocket sleeves, hand-sewed the first 500 units, and validated the idea through craft shows. Karen later licensed her patents and trademarks to a manufacturer that brought the product into Target with characters such as Jurassic Park and Paw Patrol. Although the arrangement generated approximately $4 million in first-year retail sales, Karen earned only a royalty percentage and had limited control over the brand’s direction. When the licensing business began to decline, she learned e-commerce, sourced her own inventory, and launched Super Blanky on Amazon with two SKUs. The brand generated approximately $75,000 in its first five months, reached $2.2 million in sales last year, and is now projected to more than double that revenue. items.title: #765 - She Made $1M Without Selling on Amazon
items.excerpt: Kickstarter rejected her product, but she built the same product into a million-dollar brand. Learn how viral videos and founder-led content transformed an overlooked pain point into success.
items.body: Kickstarter rejected her product, but she built the same product into a million-dollar brand. Learn how viral videos and founder-led content transformed an overlooked pain point into success. ► Watch the podcasts on YouTube: https://www.youtube.com/@Helium10SeriousSellersPodcast?sub_confirmation=1 ► Instagram: instagram.com/serioussellerspodcast ► Free Amazon Seller Chrome Extension: https://h10.me/extension ► Sign Up For Helium 10: https://h10.me/signup (Use SSP10 To Save 10% For Life) ► Learn How to Sell on Amazon: https://h10.me/ft What happens when a failed nursing student, experienced e-commerce marketer, and new mother transforms a personal frustration into a million-dollar brand? In this episode, Bradley Sutton speaks with Kate Bray, founder of Reb Relief, about the unconventional journey that led her from Amazon advertising and agency leadership to creating a product inspired by her postpartum experience. After building and testing her own prototype, Kate posted a seven-second TikTok video that went viral and a second video helped her collect approximately 1,500 email sign-ups before producing a single unit. Her launch nearly collapsed when Kickstarter rejected the product just three days before the campaign was scheduled to begin. Instead of walking away, Kate turned the rejection into a powerful marketing hook and moved the launch to Shopify. Through preorders, a local credit-union loan, and investments from strategic advisors, she raised enough to fund a $60,000 initial purchase order. Despite spending most of her career in the Amazon ecosystem, Kate has yet to launch Reb Relief on Amazon because the brand has remained consistently sold out through Shopify.
